Parent guide
Welcome
This pack is for grown-ups who read with a child aged 8–10 at home. At this age your child can read much of the story on their own. Your job changes: you become thelistener
and
the
question-asker, not the teacher. You need ten to ﬁfteen minutes and the three stories in this book.
Each story is a Jurassic English original. You can read it here on paper, or open it in the free online reader at books.jurassicenglish.com, where every page has itspictures, read-to-me audio and a question.
At Level 2 the big step is evidence. Your child learns to say what they think, why, and where
in
the
story they found it: "I think … because on page 3 it says …".
How
to
read
together
When What
you
do About
Before Read the cover line together. Ask: "What do you predict?What clue made you think that?" 1 minute
During Your child reads one page aloud. You ask the Talk
togetherquestion. Ask: "Which sentence tells you?" 8 minutes
After Ask one of the four thinking questions below. Ask for apage number. 3 minutes
Finish Colour one box on the progress chart. 1 minute
Three
small
rules
1. Let
your
child
read. Help only with a word after they have tried it twice.
2. Ask
"where
does
it
say
that?" A page number turns an opinion into evidence.
3. Diﬀerent
answers
can
both
be
right if each has a clue from the story.
The
four
thinking
questions
Every Jurassic English lesson follows the same four steps, the Jurassic Thinking Cycle. Here they are in everyday words.
Step Ask
your
child Listen
for
Look
closely (Analyze) "What happened, and how do you know? Show me thesentence." A detail with a page number
What
matters? (Evaluate) "Was it fair? Was it a good choice? What is your view?" A clear view, even "not sure"
Say
why (Justify) "Why? Use because, and give a clue from the story." "I think … because on page … it says …"
What
did
we
learn? (Reﬂect) "When could this happen in real life? What would you do?" A link to their own world
A strong answer at Level 2 has three parts: a view, a reason, and a clue.
The
ﬁfteen-minute
routine
Read one story for two weeks.
Day Week
1 Week
2
Monday Your child reads the whole story. Talk together on everypage. Your child retells the story in their own words.
Tuesday Read again. Do Word
fossils. Read again. Ask the four thinking questions.
Wednesday Pages 1–3: ﬁnd one clue on each page. Think
it
through activity.
Thursday Pages 4–6: what caused what? Listen in the online reader, then talk about the ending.
Friday Put
the
story
in
order. I
can check, then colour the progress chart.
Six weeks, three stories: The Bell That Rang Too Early, then The Rain on Platform Seven, then Mango, the Market Cat. Mango is a brand-new story, printed in this packahead of its online pictures.
When
it
feels
hard
My
child
guesses
without
a
clue. Say: "Good idea. Now let's ﬁnd the sentence that shows it."
My
child
says
"I
don't
know". Oﬀer two choices: "Was it fair, or not fair?" Then ask why.
My
English
is
not
strong. Ask the questions in Vietnamese and let your child answer in English if they can. The thinking is what matters.
My
child
reads
too
fast. Ask them to read one page again "like a detective", looking for one clue.
What
you
will
see
After a few weeks most children start to give reasons without being asked, point to the page that proves their idea, and notice that a ﬁrst guess can be wrong. Keep theactivity pages; they show how your child's reasoning grows.

Market
morning
Every Saturday, Pavi helped her uncle at the small town market. Her job was to ring a brass bell when the stalls were ready.
Ren, the new boy, liked to draw. He drew a ﬁsh stall, a ﬂower stall and Uncle’s mountain of hats.
‘You need a real job,’ said Pavi. ‘We all have to be useful.’
Ren closed his sketchbook. He sat behind the hats.

The
wrong
time
Pavi checked the stalls. Flowers: ready. Fish: ready. Hats: nearly ready.
Then the bell rang. People came through the gate. A basket fell. Uncle ran to help.
‘Ren!’ Pavi said. ‘You wanted a job. Did you ring it?’
Ren shook his head. ‘I was here.’
Pavi looked at his closed sketchbook. That did not prove where he had been.

together.
